title: What Is a Human Being?
subtitle: Body and soul, the image of God, and what we are made of, with each serious view stated by its own best defenders
triageNote: That human beings are made in the image of God and matter infinitely is shared first-order ground. It is the floor under every Christian. But how that image is defined, and how the body and soul relate, are questions where faithful believers who love the same Lord have differed for centuries. You can be wrong about the wiring of a human person and still be saved. Still holy. Still right about the One who made you.
question: When you look in the mirror, what exactly are you looking at? Are you a body with a soul tucked inside it, a kind of ghost driving a machine? Are you simply a body, a living physical creature with no separate part that floats free when you die? Or are you something stranger and more unified than either picture, a single living whole where soul and body are not two stacked things but one mystery? And when you die, before the resurrection, is there a you that is awake and with the Lord? Or do you sleep until the trumpet sounds? Almost every believer has stood at a graveside and wondered where the person went. This debate lives inside that question.
whyItMatters:
If you are new to faith, this can sound like a puzzle for philosophers with nothing better to do. It is not. What you believe a human being is shapes how you treat human beings. And especially the ones who cannot defend themselves. Consider the dying. If a person is more than a working brain, then a body that no longer speaks or recognizes you may still house someone the Lord loves. You keep vigil accordingly. Consider the disabled. If your worth is your reason and your usefulness, the one whose mind never developed is worth less. And history is full of the horrors that follow from that math. The Christian says no. The worth was never in the wattage.

Consider the unborn. What you think makes a human a human will decide when you think one is present and protectable. Consider yourself, on the day a doctor uses a hard word about your body. Are you the thing that is failing, or are you carried by God through the failing of it? How you answer changes how you grieve, how you hope, and how you hold the hand of someone going down into the dark. This is not abstract. It is the most personal question there is. The question of what you are.

positions.name: Substance Dualism (whole-person dualism)
positions.inOneLine: A human being is a deep unity of a physical body and an immaterial soul. And the soul can keep living, even consciously, in the gap between death and the resurrection.
positions.bestCase:
Begin with the word so no one is confused. Substance dualism means a human person is made of two real kinds of thing, two substances. One is the body, which you can weigh and X-ray. The other is the soul, which we call immaterial, meaning it is not made of matter. It has no weight, takes up no space, and cannot be found with any instrument. Older defenders sometimes pictured this crudely, as if the soul were a ghost merely renting the body. We reject the crude picture. That is why many of us prefer the name whole-person dualism, the label some of our writers give it. We mean that in this life you are a profound unity. Your soul and body are wedded so closely that a headache darkens your prayers and a kindness done to your body gladdens your soul. We are not two roommates. We are one person, woven of two threads.

But they are two threads. And that matters most at the moment they come apart. We hold that the soul can exist without the body. Not happily, not completely, but really. When you die, the body goes into the ground and the soul goes to be with the Lord, awake and aware. There it stays until the day God raises the body and reunites the two forever. This conscious in-between time is what theologians call the intermediate state, the state of the person between death and resurrection.

Why do we hold this? Because Jesus told a dying criminal, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Today, not at the end of history. Because Paul said that to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). And that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Paul was not longing for unconsciousness. He was longing for a presence he expected to enjoy before his body rose. Because Jesus warned us not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28). That warning assumes the two can be separated. It assumes the soul outlasts the killing of the body.

We also think this guards something precious about you. If you are more than your matter, then the slow ruin of your body is not the ruin of you. The Alzheimer's patient whose memory has gone dark is not gone. The believer in a coma is not absent from God. Your worth does not rise and fall with your brain scan, because the real you is held by God in a way no disease can reach.

We know the objection, that the Bible cares about resurrection, not about disembodied souls drifting in heaven forever, and we agree completely. The soul without a body is incomplete, a person in waiting, not a person fulfilled. Our hope is not to escape the body. Our hope is to get it back, glorified and incorruptible. We simply will not erase the conscious in-between that Scripture seems to promise to the dying. We would rather keep the comfort Jesus gave the thief than tidy it away for the sake of a cleaner theory.
advocates: much of the historic Christian tradition

positions.name: Christian Physicalism (monism)
positions.inOneLine: A human being is a single living physical creature, not a soul housed in a body, and the Christian hope is that God will raise the dead, not that an immortal soul floats free of the grave.
positions.bestCase:
Hear our name carefully before you judge us, because it gets misread. Physicalism means we believe a human being is a physical creature, made of matter, with no separate immaterial part that can survive on its own. Monism, from the word for one, names the same conviction, that you are one thing and not two. We are not materialists in the godless sense. We do not say you are merely meat or that your love and prayer are illusions. We say that everything you are, your mind, your will, your worship, your very self, is what your living body does when God breathes life into it. We call this the psychosomatic unity, a clumsy word that simply joins soul, psyche, and body, soma, into one. You do not have a body. You are a body, a living one, the kind that thinks and chooses and loves God.

We start where the Bible starts. God formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being (Genesis 2:7). Look closely. The verse does not say God put a soul into a body. It says the dust plus God's breath equals a living being, in Hebrew a living nephesh. Man does not have a soul in that verse. Man is a living soul. The breath is the gift of life from God, not a separate ghost installed inside the clay.

We hold this for a reason we think is deeply Christian. The pagan world believed the soul was naturally immortal and the body was a prison to escape. The Bible believes something better and harder. We do not have built-in immortality. We die, all of us, fully. And then God, who raised Jesus bodily from a real tomb, will raise us. Our hope is not a soul that never died. Our hope is a God who conquers death by resurrection. This is why Paul stakes everything on the empty tomb and the raised body in 1 Corinthians 15. If the dead are not raised, he says, your faith is worthless and you are still in your sins. He does not say, never mind, at least your soul survives. For Paul, no resurrection means no hope at all, which makes most sense if the soul does not simply sail on without it.

What about the dead before the resurrection? Here we hold our view honestly. Some of us speak of the dead as asleep, a word the Bible itself uses again and again for those who have died. Others of us say that for the dead, who experience no time, the next thing they know is the resurrection morning. So to die in Christ is to wake instantly in His presence, even though ages have passed for the living. Either way, the person is safe in the memory and power of God, who will not lose what He intends to raise.

We think modern science quietly supports us, not as judge over Scripture but as a witness. Everything we once filed under soul, memory, personality, moral feeling, the sense of God, turns out to be bound up with the living brain. We can now watch it happen. Damage the brain and the person changes. This does not embarrass us. It fits the believer who already knew the dust matters, that God loves bodies. Salvation ends not in escape but in a new creation, with new bodies on a renewed earth.

positions.name: Thomistic Hylomorphism (the soul as the form of the body)
positions.inOneLine: The soul is the form of the body, so the two are not two things stacked together but one living whole. And the soul can persist after death yet remains incomplete until the body rises.
positions.bestCase:
Our view has a hard name, so let us earn it slowly. Hylomorphism comes from two Greek words, hyle for matter and morphe for form. It is the old insight of Aristotle, taken up and baptized by Thomas Aquinas, that every living thing is matter shaped by a form. The matter is the stuff. The form is the organizing principle that makes that stuff a living, particular kind of thing rather than a pile. For a human being, the soul just is the form of the body. The soul is not a passenger riding inside the body and it is not a ghost that happens to be parked there. The soul is what makes your body a living human body at all, the inner principle by which dust stands up and thinks and loves.

Notice what this does. It refuses both of the other pictures and keeps what is true in each. Against the crude dualist, we say you are not two things loosely joined, a soul wearing a body like a coat. You are one thing, one substance, body and soul together as matter and form of a single whole. When you stub your toe, it is not that your body hurts and informs your soul. You hurt, all of you. Because you are one. Against the physicalist, we say the soul is real and is not reducible to the chemistry of the brain. Because the form of a thing is not just one more part of the thing. The shape of a statue is not a chunk of the marble. The soul is not a chunk of the body.

Now the part that makes us strange and, we think, faithful. The human soul is the kind of form that can perform acts that go beyond matter, abstract thought and free choice and the knowledge of God. So it does not simply stop when the body fails. At death the soul persists. Aquinas says it survives. But, and this is everything, the surviving soul is not the whole person. It is incomplete, a fragment longing for its body, a form without its matter. The separated soul is not you fully. It is the part of you that God preserves until He gives you back your body in the resurrection. Then the whole person stands again. So we hold a real intermediate state, that conscious gap between death and resurrection, without ever pretending the soul alone is the destination. The soul without the body is a person interrupted, waiting to be made whole.

Why hold this harder, stranger view? Because it honors all the Scriptures at once. It honors Genesis 2:7, where dust and breath make one living being, since the soul is the form of that dust, not a stranger to it. It honors the resurrection hope of 1 Corinthians 15, because the soul alone is incomplete and aches for the body. And it honors the words of Jesus to the thief and Paul's longing to depart and be with Christ, because the soul truly persists and is truly with the Lord. We do not have to choose between the unity of the person and the survival of the soul. We hold both, the way the Church largely held both for centuries before the modern arguments hardened into camps.
advocates: the Catholic and much of the classical theological tradition

biblicalEvidence.summary: The Lord formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being, a living nephesh. Dust plus God's breath equals a living creature.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Dualists answer that the verse names two ingredients, the dust and the divine breath. They read the breath of life as more than oxygen, the God-given animating principle that grounds the soul. Hylomorphists say this is their text exactly. The soul as the form of the dust is precisely how dust becomes a living being rather than a separate spirit inserted into clay.

biblicalEvidence.summary: God said, let us make man in our image, after our likeness, and let them have dominion. So God created man in His own image, male and female He created them. The imago Dei, the image of God, is stamped on the human creature.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: All three views affirm the image of God and read it as the source of human dignity. They divide instead on what the image is, whether it names our capacities like reason, our royal role as God's representatives who exercise dominion, or our capacity for relationship. The verse settles that we bear the image. It does not by itself settle whether we are one substance or two.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear Him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Jesus distinguishes the body that men can kill from the soul that they cannot.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Physicalists argue the word translated soul here is the Hebrew and Greek term for life or the whole self, not a separable immaterial part, and Jesus' point is that human enemies can take your earthly life but not your standing before God, who alone holds your final destiny. Hylomorphists read it as confirming that the soul persists even when the body is killed, which fits their teaching that the form survives the loss of its matter.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus tells the dying thief, truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise. Today, not at the distant resurrection. The man would be consciously with Christ.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Some physicalists move the comma and read it as, truly I say to you today, you will be with me in paradise. That makes today modify the speaking rather than the arrival. Others say that for the dead, who pass through no time, the next conscious moment simply is the resurrection, so today is true from the thief's side even if ages pass for the living. Dualists and hylomorphists take the plain sense, a conscious reunion that very day.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul is torn, desiring to depart and be with Christ, which is far better. He expects that dying brings him into Christ's presence in a way better than his present embodied life.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Physicalists say Paul speaks of his certain hope, not a timeline. Being with Christ is so sure that the unconscious interval, or the timeless leap to resurrection, makes departing genuinely far better. It requires no soul awake apart from the body. Dualists and hylomorphists read it straightforwardly as Paul expecting conscious fellowship with Christ between his death and his rising.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul says that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. And he would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. He also longs not to be found naked or unclothed, but further clothed with our heavenly dwelling.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Physicalists seize on the very same naked and unclothed language, arguing Paul dreads a bodiless state and longs to be clothed with the resurrection body. That shows he did not regard a disembodied soul as the goal, or even as a comfortable condition. Dualists reply that Paul plainly contemplates being away from the body and with the Lord. He calls that interval good even while he longs for the better, fuller clothing of resurrection. Hylomorphists hear their own view, a real but incomplete separated state that aches to be reclothed.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Thomistic Hylomorphism (the soul as the form of the body)
biblicalEvidence.summary: At death the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. The body goes to the ground. The life-spirit goes back to its Giver.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Physicalists note the spirit, ruach, also means breath. They read this as the God-given breath of life returning to God, an echo of Genesis 2:7 rather than a conscious soul going to heaven. Dualists read it as the soul returning to God's keeping. Hylomorphists see the body and its form parting at death, the form preserved by God until the dust is raised and reunited with it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ is not raised, our preaching is in vain, and we are still in our sins. The hope is a raised body, sown perishable and raised imperishable, a spiritual body.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Physicalists stress that Paul rests the entire faith on bodily resurrection, not on an immortal soul, since he says that without the raising of the body all is lost. Dualists fully agree resurrection is the goal and answer that affirming a conscious soul in the meantime takes nothing away from it, the soul being incomplete until the body rises. Hylomorphists read this as their own emphasis, the separated soul longing for the body that 1 Corinthians 15 promises.

weighing:
What follows is my own reading, offered as one pastor's judgment and not a verdict the Church has settled. Hold it loosely. Saints far wiser than I am have rested in each of these positions. And I have prayed beside dying believers of all three while none of them, in that hour, cared which book they had read.

When I sit with the whole of Scripture, two pulls work on me at once. I refuse to release either. The physicalists are right about the center of gravity. The Bible's hope is resurrection, not escape. We are dust that God loves, and salvation ends with new bodies on a renewed earth, not with souls drifting in a disembodied forever. Genesis 2:7 really does say man became a living being, and 1 Corinthians 15 really does stake everything on the empty tomb. Any view of the human person that treats the body as a husk to shed has wandered off from the Bible and toward Plato. So I will not let go of the unity of the person or the weight of the resurrection.

And yet I cannot make the thief on the cross disappear, and I will not try. When Jesus says today you will be with me in paradise, and when Paul aches to depart and be with Christ, they seem to me to promise something to the dying that the strict physicalist has to work very hard to keep. The reinterpretations are possible. They are not, to my ear, the most natural reading. So I find myself drawn to the position that holds both pulls at once without snapping either, and to my mind that is the hylomorphist instinct that Aquinas guarded. The soul is the form of the body, so we are one and not two, which honors the physicalist. But the form persists when the body fails, incomplete and aching for its resurrection, which honors the dying thief.

So here is my tentative resting place. I lean toward the human being as a profound unity in which the soul is no mere passenger, against the picture of a ghost in a machine. But I keep a real and conscious intermediate state, because I think the dying Christ gave the dying thief a comfort I have no authority to take back. I hold the unity of the person in one hand and the survival of the soul in the other, and I am content to be told I have not perfectly reconciled them. Paul did not finish every sentence either. I would rather end honest than tidy.
charitableDisagreement:
If you hold a different view than the one I lean toward, here is what I want you to hear from me. The Christian physicalist is not a godless materialist sneaking unbelief into the church. He is guarding the resurrection and the goodness of the body against centuries of half-pagan talk that treated flesh as a prison and heaven as a place for naked souls. He reads Genesis and 1 Corinthians on his knees. The substance dualist is not a Platonist who despises the body. He is refusing to take from a dying believer the promise of being with the Lord today, and he is protecting the truth that the demented and the comatose are not gone. The hylomorphist is not hiding behind a hard word. He is trying, with old and careful tools, to hold the unity of the person and the survival of the soul together rather than sacrificing one to save the other. Each of them is protecting a real treasure, and each fears the others will lose it.

Is this a hill to die on? No. It is a hill to think hard on, to read carefully on, to wonder about at gravesides with people you love. The faith does not stand or fall on whether the soul is a separate substance or the form of the body. It stands on the One who was raised bodily from a borrowed tomb and who promises to raise you too. A physicalist and a dualist who both trust the risen Christ will, on the resurrection morning, find they were arguing about the wiring of a house they were both about to be given new and whole. Do not let a second-order question fool you into treating a brother who bears the image of God as an enemy.

relatedDebates.topic: What the image of God actually is
relatedDebates.note: All Christians affirm that humans bear the imago Dei, the image of God. They differ on what it names. The structural view says the image is our capacities, the powers that set us apart, especially reason, conscience, and the freedom to choose, the inner equipment that makes us like God. The functional or royal view says the image is a job, our role as God's appointed representatives who rule creation on His behalf. Genesis 1 ties the image directly to dominion. And ancient kings set up images of themselves to mark their reign. The relational view says the image is our capacity for relationship. On this view, we image a God who is love precisely in our being made for communion with Him and one another, male and female together. Many today hold these as facets of one truth rather than rivals, since a creature with the capacities can do the work and live in the relationship.

relatedDebates.topic: Where the soul comes from, creationism versus traducianism
relatedDebates.note: If a human being has a soul, where does each one come from? Creationism of the soul, not to be confused with creation in the science debate, holds that God directly creates a fresh soul for each person. Most say this happens at conception. It guards the soul's special origin from God. Traducianism holds that the soul comes from the parents along with the body. It is transmitted in the act of conception, like everything else a child inherits. It explains more easily how original sin passes to every child and how a child can resemble a parent in temperament and not only in looks. This debate matters only for the views that affirm a soul, and it remains genuinely open, with serious believers on both sides.

relatedDebates.topic: What it means that God made us male and female
relatedDebates.note: Genesis 1:27 ties the image of God closely to our being created male and female. Christians have long seen our embodied sexual difference as good, given, and meaningful rather than accidental. The man and the woman together, in their difference and their union, reflect something of God. And they are commanded to be fruitful. Christians who agree on this still discuss how much of manhood and womanhood is fixed in creation and how much is shaped by culture. And how the dignity equally shared by male and female bears on their callings. But the floor is firm. The body is not a costume. To be made male and female is part of being made in the image. And it is called very good.
